extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, probability, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and principles for using probability theory (Laplace's methods) to justify induction, assess repetition of events, and form scientific belief; includes cautions about priors, applicability, and limits (miracles, infinite extrapolation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as antecedent in routine of perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause is scientifically used to denote an antecedent stage in a routine of perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this sense force as a cause is meaningless; 'first cause' is only a limit (permanent or temporary) to knowledge. No instance in experience supports an arbitrary first cause in the popular sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof in the field of perceptions = overwhelming probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof in the field of perceptions is the demonstration of overwhelming probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logically reserve the word 'know' for conceptions and 'believe' for perceptions (example: 'I know that the angle at the circumference on any diameter of a circle is right,' but 'I believe that the sun will rise to-morrow'). Overwhelming probability drawn from past experience grounds practical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's rule of succession (formula for next-event probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event has happened p times and failed q times, the probability that it will happen the next time is (p+1)/(p+q+2); the odds in favour are (p+1) to (q+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to quantify how past repetitions affect belief in future repetition (examples: sun rising vs. hydrogen solidification). Note this calculation assumes the Laplacian a priori setup (see related entries about priors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's principle for posterior probabilities of constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a result might flow from any one of a certain number of different constitutions, all equally probable before experience, then the several probabilities of each constitution after experience being the real constitution, are proportional to the probabilities that the result would flow from each of these constitutions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basis for assigning posterior probabilities: posterior ∝ prior × likelihood (stated in Laplace's terms). The text notes historical critiques (Boole) and justifications (Edgeworth) regarding the assumption of equal a priori probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use equal a priori distribution of ignorance only when experience justifies it
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'equal distribution of our ignorance' (assigning equal a priori probability to possible constitutions) should be grounded on experience that such constants are in fact found equally often in the long run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform priors blindly: if past experience shows, for example, that coins usually have head and tail, the uniform prior over all coin 'constitutions' no longer applies. Edgeworth's digit example illustrates when equal distribution is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to verify sameness of causes before predicting repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: One must be cautious and take a sufficiently comprehensive sequence of perceptions; ensure that the causes/components are really the same before predicting repetition from past experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by river flooding example: observing two floods of a river is not enough to predict a third unless seasonal/causal conditions (season, snowmelt, banks, etc.) are the same. See Mill's Canons of Induction for fuller treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation of prior repeated sequences increases odds for a new sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have experienced m sequences each repeated n times without anomies, and a new sequence repeated r times, then the odds in favour of the new sequence repeating on the next occasion are m(n−1)+r to 1 (under the Laplace framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how accumulated, comprehensive past experience massively increases the posterior odds for routine in a new sequence; caveat: apply only when the sequences truly share the same causal components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles (breaches of routine) are practically negligible given extreme odds
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimated odds against a well-authenticated breach of routine (a 'miracle') occurring in the next sequence are enormously large (example: ~1,000 million to one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore any belief that the miraculous will occur in immediate experience cannot form a factor in practical conduct of life; such events are effectively negligible for decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of new phenomena under law of causation via overwhelming prior experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Because past experience shows many sequences follow the same routine, Laplace's theorem implies overwhelming odds that a newly observed phenomenon can be classified under the law of causation (i.e., will follow routine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports inductive generalisation: given the effectively infinite number of past routine cases, even a singly-observed successful experiment often makes repetition highly probable — but see caveats about identical causes and priors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of probabilistic inference: cannot extrapolate to infinite future
rubrics_metrics.description: We may have overwhelming odds that routine will be preserved for any finite future interval, but we cannot argue from finite past experience for an infinite future repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probabilistic proof applies to finite extrapolations only; the mathematics does not justify claims about infinite continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature (space/time) as mode of perception affects probability assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is construed as a construct of the human mind; time and space are modes of discriminating groups of sense-impressions rather than properties of an unknowable beyond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical stance grounds the assumption that 'conditions for each trial remaining the same' lie in identity of the perceptive faculty; hence probabilistic trials presuppose stability of perceptive conditions across observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priors must reflect prior knowledge or experience (avoid universal application of Laplace's a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: The result from Laplace's uniform-a priori calculation 'ceases to have application when we have once had the experience that coins usually have a head and a tail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior experience gives knowledge about the distribution of constitutions, that knowledge should inform priors rather than using a blind uniform prior; the logic of drawing information from 'complete ignorance' is questioned and requires empirical justification.
